title_en: Anhui Foreign Economic Construction Co., Ltd. v. Dongfang Zhiye Real Estate Co., Ltd. — dispute over letter of guarantee fraud, with third parties Bank of Costa Rica and China Construction Bank Corporation, Anhui Branch
ruling_gist_en: I. When determining whether independent guarantee fraud is constituted and review of the underlying transaction is involved, the principle of limited and necessary review shall be adhered to. The scope of review shall be limited to whether the beneficiary clearly knew that the counterparty to the underlying contract had not committed any breach of the underlying contract or that there was no other fact that would trigger payment under the independent guarantee. Otherwise, excessive review of the underlying contract will undermine the institutional value of the independent guarantee as a 'pay on first demand' instrument.

full_text_en:
Anhui Foreign Economic Construction (Group) Co., Ltd. v. Oriental Real Estate Co., Ltd., with Banco de Costa Rica and China Construction Bank Corporation, Anhui Branch as Third Parties — Dispute over Guarantee Fraud

【Ruling Summary】

1. When determining whether fraud in an independent guarantee involves review of the underlying transaction, the principle of limitation and necessity shall be adhered to. The scope of review shall be limited to whether the beneficiary knew that the counterparty to the underlying contract had not breached its obligations under the underlying contract or that there were no other facts triggering payment under the independent guarantee. Otherwise, excessive review of the underlying contract would undermine the institutional value of independent guarantees as "pay on first demand."

2. A breach of contract by the beneficiary under the underlying contract does not necessarily constitute fraudulent demand under the independent guarantee. That is, a breach by the beneficiary under the underlying contract is neither a sufficient nor necessary condition for guarantee fraud.

3. In determining whether fraud exists under an independent counter-guarantee, it is necessary not only to examine whether fraud exists under the independent guarantee, but also to consider whether the guarantor bank (the issuing bank of the independent guarantee) acted fraudulently when asserting its rights against the counter-guarantee issuing bank. Only when the guarantor bank, knowing that the beneficiary's demand was fraudulent and having paid in violation of the principle of good faith, subsequently demands payment from the counter-guarantee bank under the independent counter-guarantee, can it be concluded that the guarantor bank has made a fraudulent demand under the independent counter-guarantee.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2017) Supreme People's Court Civil Re-Trial No. 134

Re-Petitioner (Defendant at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Oriental Real Estate Co., Ltd. (Inmobiliaria Palacio Oriental S.A.). Address: Urbanización Jardines, San José, Republic of Costa Rica.

Representative: Ming Lan Shuen, Chairperson of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Li Yunhai, Attorney at Beijing Zhonglun Wende Law Firm.

Respondent (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): Anhui Foreign Economic Construction (Group) Co., Ltd. Address: No. 28 Dongliu Road, Baohe District, Hefei City, Anhui Province, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Jiang Qingde, Chairperson of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Ji Jingwu, Attorney at Beijing Dacheng (Haikou) Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Hou Jiayin, Attorney at Beijing Dacheng Law Firm.

Third Party at First Instance: Banco de Costa Rica. Address: 0-2 Dao 4-6, San José, Republic of Costa Rica.

Representative: Mario Barrenechea Coto, General Manager of the Bank.

Agent ad litem: Sun Fanglong, Attorney at Beijing Zhonglun (Qingdao) Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Jing Weihang, Attorney at Beijing Zhonglun (Qingdao) Law Firm.

Third Party at First Instance: China Construction Bank Corporation, Anhui Branch. Address: No. 255 Huizhou Avenue, Hefei City, Anhui Province, People's Republic of China.

Representative: Dai Yueming, President of the Branch.

Agent ad litem: Xu Ziqing, Attorney at Shanghai Jintiancheng (Hefei) Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Wang Yongjun, Attorney at Shanghai Jintiancheng (Hefei) Law Firm.

The re-petitioner, Oriental Real Estate Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Oriental Real Estate Company), filed a petition for retrial with this Court against the civil judgment (2014) Wan Min Er Zhong Zi No. 00389 of the Anhui High People's Court in the case of dispute over guarantee fraud between the respondent, Anhui Foreign Economic Construction (Group) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Foreign Economic Construction Group), and the third parties at first instance, Banco de Costa Rica and China Construction Bank Corporation, Anhui Branch (hereinafter referred to as CCB Anhui Branch). On June 3, 2016, this Court issued the civil ruling (2016) Supreme People's Court Civil Retrial No. 61, granting the retrial. After granting the retrial, this Court formed a collegiate bench in accordance with the law and held a public hearing on August 8, 2017. Li Yunhai, agent ad litem of Oriental Real Estate Company; Ji Jingwu and Hou Jiayin, agents ad litem of Foreign Economic Construction Group; Sun Fanglong and Jing Weihang, agents ad litem of Banco de Costa Rica; and Xu Ziqing, agent ad litem of CCB Anhui Branch, attended the hearing. The case is now concluded.

Foreign Economic Construction Group filed an action with the Hefei Intermediate People's Court of Anhui Province (hereinafter referred to as the court of first instance) alleging that: Oriental Real Estate Company had breached the underlying contract; while the payment obligations under the underlying contract between the parties were still at the arbitration stage and the Costa Rican court had issued an order suspending payment, Oriental Real Estate Company nevertheless applied to Banco de Costa Rica for enforcement of the independent guarantee, violating the principle of good faith and constituting an abuse of the independence principle of the guarantee, thereby amounting to fraud. The plaintiff requested a judgment: First, that the conduct of Oriental Real Estate Company constituted guarantee fraud; second, that Oriental Real Estate Company's act of claiming under the guarantee was invalid as a civil act; third, that CCB Anhui Branch should not pay the sum of USD 2,008,000 under the bank guarantee numbered 34147020000289 to Banco de Costa Rica; and fourth, that Banco de Costa Rica should not pay the sum of USD 2,008,000 under the bank guarantee numbered G051225 to Oriental Real Estate Company.

The court of first instance found the following facts:

On January 16, 2010, Oriental Real Estate Company, as the developer, entered into the "Construction Contract for the Lakeside Huafu Project in Costa Rica" (hereinafter referred to as the "Construction Contract") in San José, Republic of Costa Rica, with Foreign Economic Construction Group as the contractor and Anhui Foreign Economic Construction Central America Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Foreign Economic Construction Central America) as the construction party. The construction scope of the contractor was stipulated as: three fourteen-story comprehensive commercial and residential buildings, three basement floors, with a total area of approximately 35,516.8 square meters, including 9,909 square meters of underground structure, 25,607.8 square meters of above-ground structure, and redirection of rainwater pipelines. After the contract was signed, on May 26, 2010, Foreign Economic Construction Group applied to CCB Anhui Branch, and with Banco de Costa Rica as the re-issuing bank, a performance guarantee was issued in favor of Oriental Real Estate Company as the beneficiary, with the guaranteed matter being the Costa Rica Lakeside Huafu Project. On May 28, 2010, Banco de Costa Rica issued a performance guarantee numbered G051225, with the guarantor being CCB Anhui Branch, the principal being Foreign Economic Construction Group, the beneficiary being Oriental Real Estate Company, and the guaranteed amount being USD 2,008,000, valid until October 12, 2011, later extended to February 12, 2012. CCB Anhui Branch simultaneously issued a counter-guarantee numbered 34147020000289 to Banco de Costa Rica, undertaking to pay the amount under the guarantee within twenty days of receiving a notice from Banco de Costa Rica.

On February 7, 2012, Foreign Economic Construction Central America submitted an arbitration request to the Dispute Resolution Center of the Costa Rican Association of Architects and Engineers against Oriental Real Estate Company as the respondent, requesting the arbitral tribunal to rule on termination of the contract and to award damages of USD 1,213,487.30 to Foreign Economic Construction Central America, on the grounds that Oriental Real Estate Company had seriously breached the contract by failing to pay the progress payments for completed work and the corresponding interest. On February 10, 2012, Banco de Costa Rica sent a telex to CCB Anhui Branch, stating that Oriental Real Estate Company had made a claim demanding payment of USD 2,008,000 under Bank Guarantee No. G051225, and therefore requiring CCB Anhui Branch to pay the said amount before February 16, 2012. On February 12, upon application by Foreign Economic Construction Central America, the Second Chamber of the Administrative Litigation Court of Costa Rica issued a temporary protective measures order, ruling that Banco de Costa Rica should suspend execution of the performance guarantee No. G051225.

On February 23, 2012, Foreign Economic Construction Group filed an action for guarantee fraud with the court of first instance, and simultaneously applied for an order to suspend payment under Guarantee No. G051225 and Counter-Guarantee No. 34147020000289. On February 27, the court of first instance issued the ruling (2012) He Min Si Chu Zi No. 00005-1, ordering the suspension of payment under Guarantee No. G051225 and Counter-Guarantee No. 34147020000289, and served the ruling to CCB Anhui Branch on February 28. On February 29, CCB Anhui Branch sent a telex to Banco de Costa Rica informing it of the ruling made by the court of first instance, and on the same day sent a copy of the ruling to Banco de Costa Rica, which received the copy of the ruling on March 5.

On March 6, 2012, the Second Chamber of the Administrative Litigation Court of Costa Rica ruled against Foreign Economic Construction Central America's application for preventive measures, lifting the temporary protective measures order. On March 16, 2012, Banco de Costa Rica sent a telex to CCB Anhui Branch, stating its decision to suspend payment under Guarantee No. G051225 until the dispute was resolved, and expressly stated, "Once the Chinese court informs you that the dispute has been resolved, we will implement the resolution of the Chinese court," and accordingly requested CCB Anhui Branch to extend the validity period of Counter-Guarantee No. 34147020000289 until the dispute was resolved by a Chinese court. On March 20, CCB Anhui Branch extended the validity period of Counter-Guarantee No. 34147020000289, and undertook that "once a Chinese court requires us to pay the guarantee 34147020000289, we will immediately pay this amount to Banco de Costa Rica." On March 21, Banco de Costa Rica paid the amount under Guarantee No. G051225 to Oriental Real Estate Company.

On July 9, 2013, the Costa Rican Association of Architects and Engineers ruled that Oriental Real Estate Company had seriously breached the contract during performance, and ordered Oriental Real Estate Company to pay Foreign Economic Construction Central America progress payments for Stages 1 to 18 totaling USD 800,058.45 plus interest. Foreign Economic Construction Group believed that Oriental Real Estate Company had violated the principle of good faith, abused the independence principle of the guarantee, and constituted fraud.

The court of first instance held that:

The issues in dispute in this case were: (1) the jurisdiction and applicable law of this case; (2) whether Oriental Real Estate Company's conduct constituted guarantee fraud; and (3) what legal liabilities should be borne by Banco de Costa Rica and CCB Anhui Branch.

(1) The guarantee legal relationship in this case involved four parties. Foreign Economic Construction Group, as the domestic parent company of Foreign Economic Construction Central America, was the applicant for the issuance of the guarantee at issue. It applied to CCB Anhui Branch to issue a demand counter-guarantee in favor of Banco de Costa Rica, which then re-issued a performance guarantee to the beneficiary Oriental Real Estate Company. The cause of action in this case was a dispute over guarantee fraud. Guarantee fraud constitutes a tort. Under the jurisdictional rules for tort actions, jurisdiction lies with the court of the defendant's domicile or the place where the tort was committed. The place where the tort was committed includes the place where the tortious act was performed and the place where the tortious result occurred. In this case, the counter-guarantor, CCB Anhui Branch, and the applicant, Foreign Economic Construction Group, are both located within the People's Republic of China, and the tortious result of the alleged guarantee fraud also occurred within China. Therefore, Foreign Economic Construction Group has the right to bring this action in China, and the court of first instance has jurisdiction. The arguments of Oriental Real Estate Company and Banco de Costa Rica that Foreign Economic Construction Group had no right to bring this action in China were unfounded. Regarding the applicable law, since the guarantees at issue agreed to apply the international practice of the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees (URDG), in accordance with the principle of party autonomy, the law or practice expressly chosen by the parties shall be followed. At the same time, according to Article 44 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations, tort liability applies the law of the place where the tort was committed. Therefore, the determination of guarantee fraud and the standards for stopping payment in this case should directly apply Chinese law. As for the determination of guarantee fraud, the URDG and Chinese laws and judicial interpretations do not have explicit provisions; the relevant provisions of the United Nations Convention on Independent Guarantees and Stand-by Letters of Credit may be referred to for analysis and determination.

(2) According to the provisions of the URDG, an independent guarantee has a documentary character. That is, when the guarantor exercises reasonable care in examining the documents presented by the beneficiary, it only needs to examine whether the documents strictly comply with the terms of the guarantee and whether the documents are consistent on their face. It does not need to examine the performance of the underlying contract. At the same time, while international practices and conventions recognize the independence of independent guarantees, based on the principle of good faith, fraudulent claims are an important defense for the guarantor to refuse payment even if the documents appear on their face to comply, i.e., the fraud exception defense. International conventions list several circumstances of the fraud exception, including the circumstance that "from the type and purpose of the guarantee it can be concluded that the beneficiary's claim has no conceivable basis; the guarantor may, in accordance with the principle of good faith, exercise the fraud exception defense and refuse to pay the beneficiary." Therefore, when a court hears a dispute over guarantee fraud, it must conduct a necessary review of the performance of the underlying contract. Especially when the underlying contract has been the subject of a final judgment or award by a foreign court or arbitral institution, the facts found by the foreign institution may be used as evidence to determine the performance of the underlying contract.

Based on the facts found by the arbitration award of the Dispute Resolution Center of the Costa Rican Association of Architects and Engineers, Oriental Real Estate Company had seriously breached the contract during performance and should pay Foreign Economic Construction Central America progress payments for Stages 1 to 18 totaling USD 800,058.45 and corresponding interest. The purpose of the performance guarantee in this case was to ensure that Foreign Economic Construction Central America could perform the construction contract in accordance with the terms. Oriental Real Estate Company failed to adduce evidence to prove that Foreign Economic Construction Central America had materially breached the contract during performance. Moreover, Oriental Real Estate Company, knowing that Foreign Economic Construction Central America had submitted the contractual dispute to arbitration, abused its right to claim under the guarantee, violating the fundamental principle of good faith and constituting a fraudulent claim. Therefore, its claim was invalid, and Banco de Costa Rica should terminate payment of the amount under the guarantee.

(3) The court of first instance had issued an order suspending payment under the guarantee before Banco de Costa Rica actually made payment to Oriental Real Estate Company, ordering Banco de Costa Rica and CCB Anhui Branch to suspend payment under the performance guarantee and counter-guarantee. After receiving the order, CCB Anhui Branch had informed Banco de Costa Rica of the order by telex and sent a copy of the ruling. Despite knowing that the court of first instance had issued an order suspending payment and having undertaken to CCB Anhui Branch to suspend payment until the dispute was resolved by a Chinese court, Banco de Costa Rica still violated the above order and unilaterally paid Oriental Real Estate Company, clearly violating the principle of good faith, which is an internationally accepted practice. Banco de Costa Rica should bear the corresponding legal consequences for its own actions. The court of first instance had already determined that Oriental Real Estate Company's claim constituted fraud and was invalid. Therefore, CCB Anhui Branch should terminate payment of the amount under the counter-guarantee to Banco de Costa Rica. However, since Banco de Costa Rica had actually paid the amount under the guarantee to Oriental Real Estate Company in violation of the suspension order, Foreign Economic Construction Group's claim for an order that Banco de Costa Rica terminate payment under the guarantee had no factual basis.

In summary, the court, in accordance with Article 4 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, and Articles 3 and 44 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations, rendered the civil judgment (2012) He Min Si Chu Zi No. 00005, ordering: (1) Oriental Real Estate Company's claim under the performance guarantee No. G051225 constituted fraud; (2) CCB Anhui Branch shall terminate payment of USD 2,008,000 under the bank guarantee numbered 34147020000289 to Banco de Costa Rica; (3) Foreign Economic Construction Group's other claims were denied. The case acceptance fee was RMB 97,693, and the property preservation fee was RMB 5,000, totaling RMB 102,693, to be borne by Oriental Real Estate Company.

Oriental Real Estate Company, dissatisfied with the judgment of first instance, appealed to the Anhui High People's Court (hereinafter referred to as the court of second instance), arguing that:

USD 2,008,000.

The court of second instance, upon trial, confirmed the facts found by the court of first instance.

The court of second instance additionally found: Article 19 of the Construction Contract involved stipulated that if the developer fails to pay the project payment (progress payment) in accordance with the contract, and the parties fail to reach an agreement on payment extension, causing the construction to be unable to proceed, the contractor may stop construction until payment is made, and all losses and damages incurred by the contractor arising therefrom shall be borne by the developer. If construction is stopped for more than 28 days and the developer still fails to pay the progress payment, the contractor has the right to rescind the contract without assuming any liability, and in such case, the developer shall compensate for all losses and damages caused. Article 20 stipulated that the guarantee scope of the performance bond No. G051225 issued by Banco de Costa Rica to Orient Development Company and the counter-guarantee No. 34147020000289 issued by CCB Anhui Branch to Banco de Costa Rica is: the quality and durability of materials used during the construction period, compensation or indemnification for losses, and/or payment for the contractor's failure to perform its obligations.

On February 8, 2012, Orient Development Company submitted a claim statement and a statement of default to Banco de Costa Rica, stating: whereas the construction quality of COVEC Central America Company is inferior and fails to meet standards, the cost of necessary modifications is substantial and still unquantifiable, and the company has failed to fulfill the basic requirements for good construction, thereby violating Article V(20) of the default clause in the Construction Contract, making it impossible to meet the project inspection requirements and affecting the construction schedule. At the same time, it submitted the "Project Inspection Report" signed by architects Jose Brenes and Mauricio Mora of AIA International Architects on January 23, 2012.

It was further found: The arbitral award made by the Dispute Resolution Center of the Association of Architects and Engineers of Costa Rica on July 9, 2013, determined that until mid-2011, the contract was executed relatively normally; the developer's requests or objections were adopted by the contractor, and progress payments were never stopped until the 17th installment. In December 2011, the 18th progress payment was analyzed and approved by the supervisor, but was not made. According to the financial report submitted by COVEC Central America Company, the total amount of outstanding invoices was USD 800,058.45, and the contractor and applicant fulfilled their contractual obligations up to the 18th progress schedule, including the rectification of defective construction or payment of related expenses. From December 2011 to early January 2012, the contractor withdrew from the project site, and the contractor initiated the claim procedure before withdrawal. The 19th phase of the work was not accepted by the developer, and the inspectors had doubts about the construction quality. In view of Orient Development Company's material breach, the Construction Contract signed on January 18, 2010, was terminated; Orient Development Company was ordered to pay COVEC Central America Company a total of USD 800,058.45 for the 1st to 18th phases of project payments.

The court of second instance held:

The issues in dispute in this case are: (1) whether the facts found by the court of first instance were clear; (2) whether the application of law by the court of first instance was erroneous; (3) whether Orient Development Company's conduct constituted guarantee fraud; and (4) whether Banco de Costa Rica's undertaking to resolve the guarantee in accordance with the Chinese court's solution constitutes a sufficient condition for terminating payment under the guarantee.

(1) The Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT) is a non-profit international cooperative organization among banks, aimed at providing fast and secure services for banks and other financial institutions to complete financial transactions through electronic message exchange. Major commercial banks in China and banks in most countries around the world have joined the organization as member banks. SWIFT messages are authentic, valid, monitorable, and authoritative. Once transaction data of member banks enters the SWIFT system, banks and their head offices can query and retrieve it through the system. Although the organization's headquarters and data exchange center are located outside China, the SWIFT messages submitted by COVEC Group and CCB Anhui Branch originated from computers within China, not from abroad, and therefore do not require certification through diplomatic channels. Furthermore, the SWIFT messages in question are reliable in terms of generation, storage, and transmission methods, the completeness of their content is maintained, and the methods for identifying the sender and recipient are reliable. Pursuant to Article 5 of the Electronic Signature Law of the People's Republic of China, these messages should be deemed as originals of evidence, and their source, storage, and content have been notarized by a notary public, thus possessing authenticity, relevance, and legality. There was no impropriety in the court of first instance's finding of facts based on the above SWIFT messages. Although Orient Development Company submitted a project inspection report signed by architects of AIA International Architects, stating that the construction quality of COVEC Central America Company was poor, the arbitral award made by the Dispute Resolution Center of the Association of Architects and Engineers of Costa Rica submitted by COVEC Group did not find that COVEC Central America Company had materially breached the contract. In the face of conflicts between the "Project Inspection Report" issued by AIA International Architects and the facts found by the arbitral tribunal in its arbitral award, the court of first instance, in accordance with Article 77 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Proceedings, had legal and factual basis for finding, based on the arbitral award, that COVEC Central America Company did not commit a material breach in performing the Construction Contract. Therefore, Orient Development Company's ground of appeal that the facts found by the court of first instance were erroneous could not be sustained, and the court did not adopt it.

(2) The counter-guarantee No. 34147020000289 issued by CCB Anhui Branch to Banco de Costa Rica expressly stipulated compliance with the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees published by the International Chamber of Commerce. The guarantee rules are not limited to the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees alone; there are domestic laws, international practices, and international conventions for the parties to choose from. The Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees, as an international practice, apply only if the parties to the guarantee expressly stipulate their application. In this case, the parties to the guarantee expressly agreed to their application, and therefore the parties' will should be respected, and compliance should be maintained in all aspects concerning the issuance, amendment, conditions for claim, and guarantor's review obligations of the guarantee and counter-guarantee. Given that the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees require very simple documents to be submitted by the beneficiary when making a claim, the possibility of fraud is relatively high. However, neither the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees nor China's domestic laws provide for the determination of guarantee fraud and exceptions to guarantee fraud. The United Nations Convention on Independent Guarantees and Stand-by Letters of Credit reflects the general rules for the operation of independent guarantees and standby letters of credit in international trade practice. These rules have been widely recognized by the international community. Even if China has not acceded to the Convention, its guiding role for parties using independent guarantees cannot be denied. Therefore, it was not improper for the court of first instance to refer to the provisions of the United Nations Convention on Independent Guarantees and Stand-by Letters of Credit concerning guarantee fraud in handling this case. Although the judgment of the first instance did not specify the specific articles of the Convention applied, a comparison with the Convention shows that the circumstance cited in the judgment of the first instance – "if it can be determined from the type and purpose of the guarantee that the beneficiary's claim is without any basis, the guarantor may, in accordance with the principle of good faith, exercise the defense of fraud exception and refuse to pay the beneficiary" – is provided in Article 19 of the Convention under "Exception to the Obligation to Pay." The court of first instance's mere indication that it referred to the United Nations Convention on Independent Guarantees and Stand-by Letters of Credit without citing specific articles does not constitute an error in the application of law and has no impact on the outcome of the judgment. Therefore, Orient Development Company's ground of appeal that the application of law by the court of first instance was erroneous could not be sustained, and the court did not adopt it.

(3) According to the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees, when the guarantor examines the documents presented by the beneficiary, as long as the documents are in complete conformity with the terms of the guarantee and are consistent on their face with each other, the guarantor must assume the primary obligation to pay, without the need to examine the authenticity or validity of the documents, the performance of the underlying contract, etc. This documentary characteristic of independent guarantees provides an opportunity for the beneficiary to make fraudulent claims. To prevent guarantee fraud, in accordance with the principle of good faith, international practices and international conventions, while recognizing the independence of independent guarantees, treat fraudulent claims as an important defense for the guarantor to refuse payment, i.e., the fraud exception defense. Therefore, when a court hears a guarantee fraud dispute, to determine whether fraud exists, it is necessary to examine whether the applicant of the guarantee had breached the underlying contract in performing it. Given that an independent guarantee only protects the beneficiary's right to claim against the guarantor, the applicant of the guarantee, when filing a lawsuit for guarantee fraud against the beneficiary, must bear the burden of proving that the beneficiary committed fraud. If the applicant can prove that it has fully and properly performed its obligations under the underlying contract, or that its breach was caused by the willful misconduct of the beneficiary of the guarantee, then the beneficiary's payment request may be found to constitute fraud. If the applicant merely alleges that the beneficiary had breached the underlying contract without proving that it had fully and properly performed its contractual obligations, the beneficiary's payment request does not constitute fraud. In this case, the claim statement and statement of default submitted by Orient Development Company to Banco de Costa Rica specified that the specific facts of COVEC Central America Company's breach were that the construction quality was poor, violating Article V(20) of the Construction Contract. However, the arbitral award made by the Dispute Resolution Center of the Association of Architects and Engineers of Costa Rica submitted by COVEC Group did not find that COVEC Central America Company's construction involved a material breach; instead, it found that the contractor and applicant had performed their contractual obligations up to the 18th progress schedule, including the rectification of defective construction or payment of related expenses. Additionally, according to Article 19 of the Construction Contract, since Orient Development Company failed to pay the 18th progress payment, which was analyzed and approved by the supervisor, COVEC Central America Company was entitled to stop construction without assuming liability. Although Orient Development Company submitted a notarial certificate issued by a Costa Rican notary after the hearing, stating that the Fourth Civil Court of San Jose, Costa Rica had accepted the lawsuit filed by Orient Development Company against COVEC Central America Company regarding the Construction Contract, and that the court declared COVEC Central America Company in contempt and in default of Orient Development Company's claims on September 10, 2014, purporting to prove COVEC Central America Company's breach, the declaration of default was based on COVEC Central America Company's failure to answer within the statutory period, not on a finding of actual breach. Therefore, Orient Development Company had no reasonable basis for demanding payment under the guarantee from Banco de Costa Rica, and its demand constituted fraud. Its ground of appeal in this regard lacked sufficient factual basis, and the court did not accept it.

(4) Article 19 of the United Nations Convention on Independent Guarantees and Stand-by Letters of Credit provides that in the exceptional circumstances where payment may not be required, the principal/applicant of the guarantee is entitled to apply for interim judicial measures to prevent the guarantor/issuer from paying the beneficiary. The court of first instance, upon COVEC Group's application, issued Civil Ruling (2012) He Min Si Chu Zi No. 00005-1, intending to prevent the guarantor/issuer from paying the beneficiary. Pursuant to Article 267 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, when serving legal documents on a party without domicile within the territory of China, the people's court shall first serve them in the manner provided for in the international treaties concluded or jointly acceded to between the country of the recipient and China; if there is no international treaty relationship, service shall be effected through diplomatic channels. Since China and Costa Rica have not concluded or jointly acceded to an international treaty on judicial assistance, the court of first instance should have served Civil Ruling (2012) He Min Si Chu Zi No. 00005-1 on Banco de Costa Rica through diplomatic channels. The court of first instance's sending a message via CCB Anhui Branch to inform Banco de Costa Rica of the relevant facts and mailing a copy of the ruling was not in compliance with the relevant provisions of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China concerning service on foreign parties. Nevertheless, after learning of the contents of the aforementioned civil ruling and replying to CCB Anhui Branch that it "would implement according to the Chinese court's solution," Banco de Costa Rica applied to CCB Anhui Branch to extend the validity of guarantee No. 34147020000289 and paid the beneficiary under the guarantee on the day following the extension, thereby violating the internationally recognized practice of good faith and constituting non-bona fide payment. It shall bear the corresponding legal consequences of its own conduct.

In summary, none of Orient Development Company's grounds of appeal could be sustained. The court, in accordance with Article 170, paragraph 1, item 1, Article 175, Article 259, Article 264, Article 267, and Article 270 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered Civil Judgment (2014) Wan Min Er Zhong Zi No. 00389: dismissed the appeal and affirmed the original judgment. The second-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 97,493 was to be borne by Orient Development Company.

Orient Development Company, dissatisfied with the judgment of the second instance, applied to this Court for retrial, stating:

(1) The judgment of the second instance lacked evidence to support the basic facts found, falling under the circumstance provided in Article 200, paragraph 2, of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. First, COVEC Central America Company had breached the Construction Contract in performing it. Orient Development Company, in accordance with the terms of the bank guarantee, was entitled to claim the rights under the guarantee when the guarantor had breached. On May 28, 2010, Banco de Costa Rica issued performance bond No. G051225, which stipulated: "Banco de Costa Rica assumes no responsibility or commitment for the truthfulness of the reasons for enforcing the bond, nor does it involve supervision or inspection; all the above risks are borne by the parties." At the same time, CCB Anhui Branch issued counter-guarantee No. 34147020000289 to Banco de Costa Rica, stipulating: "We (CCB Anhui Branch) agree to pay you, within no more than twenty days from receipt of your notice, any amounts, including principal and financing costs, requested during the performance of the guarantee." Given that COVEC Central America Company did not fully perform the Construction Contract, Orient Development Company's application to Banco de Costa Rica for payment under the performance bond did not constitute fraud. Second, under the basic principle of performance bonds, when COVEC Central America Company fails to fully perform the Construction Contract, Orient Development Company is entitled to claim the rights under the bond without needing to prove a material breach by COVEC Central America Company. The second-instance judgment's finding that Orient Development Company failed to prove a material breach by COVEC Group and therefore had no reason to apply for payment under the performance bond, constituting fraud, confused the legal relationships under the performance bond and the construction contract. Third, the facts found in the "Project Inspection Report" issued by AIA International Architects and the "Arbitral Award" made by the arbitral tribunal were not in conflict. The second-instance judgment's finding that they were in conflict and consequently rejecting the "Project Inspection Report" was erroneous.

(2) The second-instance judgment's exclusion of the application of the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees falls under the circumstance provided in Article 200, paragraph 6, of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. The performance bond involved in this case expressly stipulated the application of the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees at the time of issuance. The second-instance judgment held that neither the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees nor China's laws or judicial interpretations contain clear provisions on the determination of guarantee fraud, and that the relevant provisions of the United Nations Convention on Independent Guarantees and Stand-by Letters of Credit could be referenced for analysis and determination, thereby directly excluding the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees that the parties had agreed to apply. This constitutes an error in the application of law. The Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees do address the determination of guarantee fraud. Fraudulent claims are manifested both as fraud by the beneficiary in the guarantee contract (presentation of forged documents) and as fraud by the beneficiary in the underlying contract (lack of valid grounds for exercising the right to claim or presentation of documents with false content). In this case, COVEC Central America Company, as the actual contractor in Costa Rica, failed to fully perform the Construction Contract. Orient Development Company has provided evidence of COVEC Central America Company's breach, and the Costa Rican arbitral tribunal also found that COVEC Central America Company had breached. Orient Development Company did not commit fraud in the underlying contract. Since COVEC Central America Company failed to fully perform the underlying contract, COVEC Group does not have the defense of fraud exception as provided in the United Nations Convention on Independent Guarantees and Stand-by Letters of Credit.

In summary, it requests the revocation of the judgments of the first and second instances, and a revision of the judgment to find that Orient Development Company's claim does not constitute fraud and that CCB Anhui Branch should pay the amount under the bank guarantee.

COVEC Group replied in defense:

(1) Orient Development Company's retrial request is erroneous. First, Orient Development Company did not file a counterclaim in the first instance, and its retrial request for confirmation that its claim under the performance bond in question does not constitute fraud should not be reviewed. Second, Orient Development Company has no right to file a claim on behalf of Banco de Costa Rica.

(2) The Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees (ICC Publication No. 458) should apply to this case, with Chinese law as the governing law, and reference may also be made to the United Nations Convention on Independent Guarantees and Stand-by Letters of Credit. The application of law by the court of second instance was correct. First, pursuant to Article 27 of the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees, the law of the place of business of the guarantor or instructing party shall be the governing law. In this case, the bank that issued the counter-guarantee, CCB Anhui Branch, has its place of business in Anhui, China. Therefore, the governing law for this case is the law of the People's Republic of China. Second, the court of second instance did not exclude the application of the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees; it merely, because the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees do not provide for possible fraudulent conduct by the beneficiary, while the United Nations Convention on Independent Guarantees and Stand-by Letters of Credit effectively addresses this aspect, and the Convention represents the general principles of commercial entities of various countries, even though China has not acceded to the Convention, the Chinese court may certainly refer to the principles established therein.

(3) Dongfang Real Estate Company fabricated facts when applying for a claim under the guarantee. The court of second instance correctly found that this constituted guarantee fraud. First, Dongfang Real Estate Company's assertion that Waijing Central America Company had breached the contract was a fabricated fact. In its statement applying for enforcement of the guarantee, Dongfang Real Estate Company stated: "Given that the construction work performed by Waijing Central America Company is of inferior quality and fails to meet standards, the costs required for rectification are substantial and cannot be estimated to date. Waijing Central America Company has failed to fulfill the basic conditions for proper construction, thereby violating Article 20 of Section V on breach of contract under the Construction Contract, and cannot meet the requirements for engineering inspection, affecting the construction schedule." The sole reason given by Dongfang Real Estate Company for enforcing the guarantee was that Waijing Central America Company's "construction work is of inferior quality, fails to meet standards, and requires substantial repair costs." This reason was false, and it is also the key to determining that Dongfang Real Estate Company committed guarantee fraud. Second, the inspection report submitted by Dongfang Real Estate Company to the issuing bank was false. The report was not issued by AIA International Architects, and Dongfang Real Estate Company did not provide the bank with the architect qualification certificates of Jose Brenes and Mauricio Mora. Third, the Arbitral Award issued by the Dispute Resolution Center of the Costa Rican Institute of Architects and Engineers terminated the Construction Contract signed by the parties. Waijing Central America Company no longer has any obligation to perform the contract. On the contrary, Dongfang Real Estate Company seriously breached the contract and should pay Waijing Central America Company USD 800,058.45. This demonstrates that there was no issue of "inferior quality, failing to meet standards" in the project in question. Fourth, to ensure project quality and progress, the developer hired a supervising engineer specifically responsible for overseeing the quality and progress of the contractor's work. Each phase of work was inspected by the supervising personnel, and only if it met quality standards could the supervising engineer approve payment of progress payments. The supervising engineer's approval payment reports also prove that there were no quality problems in the project in question.

In summary, the judgments of the first and second instances are correct, and we request that the original judgment be upheld.

Costa Rica Bank submitted its opinion, stating:

(1) The legal relationship concerning the demand guarantee in this case exists only between Dongfang Real Estate Company and Costa Rica Bank. The domiciles of both Dongfang Real Estate Company and Costa Rica Bank are outside China. Chinese courts do not have jurisdiction over the dispute in this case.

(2) Given that a court of Costa Rica has already rendered a binding judgment on the guarantee in question, it is a clear excess of authority for a Chinese court to again rule and order a stay of payment of the amounts under the said guarantee.

(3) The court of first instance failed to serve the stay order on Costa Rica Bank in accordance with the law. This is a procedural error, and the stay order has no legal effect on Costa Rica Bank.

(4) The original judgment erroneously referred to and applied the United Nations Convention on Independent Guarantees and Stand-by Letters of Credit in finding that Dongfang Real Estate Company had committed fraud. The application of law was incorrect.

(5) Costa Rica Bank had reasonable grounds to believe that Dongfang Real Estate Company had not committed fraud. Moreover, after the Costa Rican court ruled that the amounts under the guarantee in question should not be stayed, Costa Rica Bank was even more obligated to perform its payment obligations to Dongfang Real Estate Company.

(6) The evidence provided by Waijing Group Company is insufficient to prove that Dongfang Real Estate Company's payment of the guarantee constituted fraud. However, the preliminary evidence provided by Dongfang Real Estate Company can prove that Waijing Central America Company was in breach of contract.

(7) Given that Costa Rica Bank has already paid the guarantee amount to Dongfang Real Estate Company, CCB Anhui Branch should perform its obligation to reimburse Costa Rica Bank in accordance with the counter-guarantee.

(8) The judgments of the first and second instances did not order a stay of the payment by Costa Rica Bank to Dongfang Real Estate Company, but rather discharged the counter-guarantee obligation that CCB Anhui Branch should have borne to Costa Rica Bank. The first and second instance judgments erroneously found that Dongfang Real Estate Company's payment of the guarantee in question constituted fraud and ordered CCB Anhui Branch to cease payment of the amounts under the counter-guarantee in question.

In summary, we request that the judgment of the second instance be reversed and all claims of Waijing Group Company be dismissed.

CCB Anhui Branch did not submit a written opinion. During the retrial hearing of this case, CCB Anhui Branch stated its opinion, claiming that the guarantee relationship between CCB Anhui Branch and Waijing Group Company had already terminated, and it should no longer be obligated to perform under the guarantee as a surety. The first and second instance judgments found that Dongfang Real Estate Company had committed guarantee fraud, so CCB Anhui Branch's cessation of payment had a legal basis.

During the retrial of this case, Dongfang Real Estate Company submitted one piece of new evidence, namely: Civil Judgment No. 150-2016 of the Fourth Civil Court of San Jose, Republic of Costa Rica, intending to prove that this civil judgment had already found that Waijing Central America Company had committed serious breaches during the performance of the Construction Contract. Waijing Group Company did not dispute the authenticity of this evidence but argued that the judgment had not yet taken legal effect and could not be used as evidence. Waijing Group Company submitted three pieces of new evidence. They are: 1. A "Schedule of Progress Payment Details" for the first to eighteenth phases of the project in question, intending to prove that all the aforementioned schedules were approved by the supervising engineer appointed by Dongfang Real Estate Company, and that there were no quality problems in the project; 2. A "Summary of the Case" prepared by a practicing attorney in Costa Rica, explaining that after the rendering of Civil Judgment No. 150-2016 by the Fourth Civil Court of San Jose, Republic of Costa Rica, Waijing Central America Company filed an appeal, and the case is currently being heard by the Second Chamber of the High Court of San Jose, Republic of Costa Rica, intending to prove that Civil Judgment No. 150-2016 of the Fourth Civil Court of San Jose, Republic of Costa Rica, has not taken legal effect; 3. A confirmation letter and related confirmation emails issued by the American Institute of Architects, intending to prove that Jose Brenes and Mauricio Mora are not international members of the American Institute of Architects, and that the project inspection report signed by them is false. Dongfang Real Estate Company acknowledged the authenticity of the aforementioned "Schedule of Progress Payment Details" and the "Summary of the Case" but did not acknowledge the purposes for which they were intended to prove. It did not acknowledge the authenticity of the confirmation letter and related confirmation emails issued by the American Institute of Architects. This Court, upon review, considers that the purposes of evidence items 1 and 3 both pertain to the quality of the project in question and the authenticity of the "Project Inspection Report" issued by Jose Brenes and Mauricio Mora. This Court will make a comprehensive determination in light of other evidence in the case. As for the issue of whether Civil Judgment No. 150-2016 of the Fourth Civil Court of San Jose, involved in evidence 2, has taken effect, during the hearing of this case, upon questioning, all parties acknowledged the fact that the case is currently being heard by the Second Chamber of the High Court of San Jose, Republic of Costa Rica.

This Court further finds during retrial that Article 20 of the Construction Contract in this case stipulated: "The contractor shall submit to the developer a performance guarantee issued by a bank, in an amount equivalent to 10% of the total contract price, taking effect on the date of contract signing and expiring upon completion of the project. If there is a change in the contract term, the contractor shall change the expiration date. ...During or after the execution of the contract, it shall always be used to guarantee the quality and durability of materials used during construction, to compensate or remedy losses caused, and/or to pay for the contractor's failure to perform its obligations. ..." On May 28, 2010, Costa Rica Bank issued a performance guarantee numbered G051225, with the guarantor being CCB Anhui Branch, the principal being Waijing Group Company, the beneficiary being Dongfang Real Estate Company, the guaranteed amount being USD 2,008,000, with a validity period until October 12, 2011, later extended to February 12, 2012. The guarantee stated: unconditional, irrevocable, essential, demand guarantee. To enforce this guarantee, the beneficiary must submit to the Central Office Foreign Trade Department of Costa Rica Bank two copies of supporting documents specifying the reasons for enforcing this guarantee, together with a notarized declaration by the beneficiary indicating the date on which Waijing Central America Company was notified of the claim due to breach, and attach the original guarantee certificate and any amendments that have been issued. At the same time, CCB Anhui Branch issued a counter-guarantee numbered 34147020000289 to Costa Rica Bank, undertaking to pay the amount under the guarantee within twenty days of receiving notice from Costa Rica Bank. The counter-guarantee was "unconditional, irrevocable, payable on demand" and stipulated "compliance with the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees (URDG) published by the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) as Publication No. 458." From the above stipulations, it can be seen that the scope of coverage of performance guarantee No. G051225 issued by Costa Rica Bank to Dongfang Real Estate Company was: the quality and durability of materials used during construction, compensation or remedy for losses caused, and/or payment for the contractor's failure to perform obligations. The bank guarantee No. 34147020000289 issued by CCB Anhui Branch to Costa Rica Bank provided a counter-guarantee for the aforementioned performance guarantee. The above facts are undisputed by all parties.

During the performance of the Construction Contract, on January 23, 2012, architects Jose Brenes and Mauricio Mora issued a "Project Inspection Report." The report found that the construction project had instances of "poor workmanship" and "inferior quality" that required modification or repair.

On February 7, 2012, Waijing Central America Company submitted an arbitration request to the Dispute Resolution Center of the Costa Rican Institute of Architects and Engineers, naming Dongfang Real Estate Company as the respondent, requesting the arbitral tribunal to rule on termination of the contract and to award damages totaling USD 1,213,487.3 to be paid by Dongfang Real Estate Company, on the grounds that Dongfang Real Estate Company was in arrears of payment for completed work and corresponding interest, constituting a material breach. On February 8, 2012, Dongfang Real Estate Company submitted to Costa Rica Bank the documents required for payment under the guarantee, including a claim statement, a notice of breach, a declaration of breach, and the "Project Inspection Report," requesting enforcement of the guarantee.

On February 10, 2012, Costa Rica Bank sent a telex to CCB Anhui Branch, stating that Dongfang Real Estate Company had submitted a claim and requested payment of USD 2,008,000 under bank guarantee No. G051225. Costa Rica Bank further requested that CCB Anhui Branch pay the said amount by February 16, 2012. On February 12, 2012, upon the application of Waijing Central America Company, the Second Chamber of the Administrative Litigation Court of the Republic of Costa Rica issued a temporary protective measure injunction, ordering Costa Rica Bank to suspend enforcement of performance guarantee No. G051225.

On February 23, 2012, Waijing Group Company filed a lawsuit with the court of first instance concerning a guarantee fraud dispute, simultaneously applying for an order to suspend payment of the amounts under guarantee No. G051225 and counter-guarantee No. 34147020000289. Waijing Group Company argued that Dongfang Real Estate Company had already breached the contract, and that while the payment obligations under the underlying contract between the parties were still in the arbitration stage and a Costa Rican court had already issued an injunction suspending payment, Dongfang Real Estate Company nevertheless applied to Costa Rica Bank for enforcement of the said guarantee, which violated the principle of good faith and constituted an abuse of the independence principle of the guarantee, amounting to fraud. On February 27, 2012, the court of first instance issued Ruling (2012) He Min Si Chu Zi No. 00005-1, ordering the suspension of payment of amounts under guarantee No. G051225 and counter-guarantee No. 34147020000289, and served the said ruling on CCB Anhui Branch on February 28, 2012. On February 29, 2012, CCB Anhui Branch sent a telex to Costa Rica Bank informing it of the ruling issued by the court of first instance, and on the same day sent a copy of the said ruling to Costa Rica Bank, which received the copy on March 5, 2012.

On March 6, 2012, the Second Chamber of the Administrative Litigation Court of the Republic of Costa Rica ruled against Waijing Central America Company's application for preventive measures, lifting the temporary protective measure injunction. On March 20, 2012, at the request of Costa Rica Bank, CCB Anhui Branch extended the validity period of counter-guarantee No. 34147020000289. On March 21, 2012, Costa Rica Bank paid the amount under guarantee No. G051225 to Dongfang Real Estate Company.

On July 9, 2013, the Costa Rican Institute of Architects and Engineers issued an arbitral award. The arbitral award also contained relevant statements regarding the project quality issue, namely: "The progress payment for the 19th phase was not approved by the supervisor and the developer," and "The facts show that the contractor has repeatedly received notices that the project works were substandard or defective. For those project works, the contractor must make improvements itself or have them corrected by other subcontractors. The problem with the external cement plastering of the building was particularly prominent. During the contract performance period, up to the 18th phase, no instances of the developer withholding the contractor's performance bond were found." The arbitral award found that Dongfang Real Estate Company had committed serious breaches during the performance of the contract and ruled to terminate the Construction Contract. It ordered Dongfang Real Estate Company to pay Waijing Central America Company the progress payments for phases 1 to 18 totalling USD 800,058.45 plus interest. The claim for payment for phase 19 was not supported because it had not been accepted by the developer. Since the amount under guarantee No. G051225 had already been paid, the request by Waijing Central America Company for return of the guarantee was not supported.

On April 9, 2014, the court of first instance in this case rendered Civil Judgment (2012) He Min Si Chu Zi No. 00005, finding that Dongfang Real Estate Company's claim under performance guarantee No. G051225 constituted fraud, and ordering CCB Anhui Branch to cease payment of the amount of USD 2,008,000 under bank guarantee No. 34147020000289 to Costa Rica Bank.

This Court additionally finds that after the arbitral award was issued by the Costa Rican Institute of Architects and Engineers, Dongfang Real Estate Company requested the First Chamber of the Supreme Court of the Republic of Costa Rica to declare the award invalid. On May 21, 2015, the First Chamber of the Supreme Court of the Republic of Costa Rica rendered a decision dismissing Dongfang Real Estate Company's request.

Except for the facts found above, all other facts found by this Court during retrial are consistent with the facts found in the original trial.

Opinion of the Court:

The parties in dispute in this case, Dongfang Real Estate Company and Costa Rica Bank, have their habitual residences outside China. This case is a foreign-related commercial dispute. Pursuant to Article 8 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations, which provides that "the characterization of a foreign-related civil relation shall be governed by the law of the forum," Waijing Group Company, as the domestic parent company of Waijing Central America Company, is the applicant for the issuance of the guarantee in question. It applied to CCB Anhui Branch to issue a demand counter-guarantee to Costa Rica Bank, which then issued a performance guarantee to the beneficiary, Dongfang Real Estate Company. According to the content of the guarantee documents, the payment obligations of Costa Rica Bank and CCB Anhui Branch are both independent of the underlying transaction relationship and the guarantee application legal relationship. Therefore, the said guarantee can be determined as an independent demand guarantee, and the said counter-guarantee can be determined as an independent demand counter-guarantee. Waijing Group Company filed a lawsuit with the court of first instance on the ground of guarantee fraud, and the nature of this case is a guarantee fraud dispute. The independent counter-guarantee whose payment was requested to be stayed was issued by CCB Anhui Branch, and the location of that branch shall be deemed the place where the tortious result claimed by Waijing Group Company occurred. The court of first instance, as the court of the place of the tort, has jurisdiction over this case. Since the guarantee in question states that it is subject to the Uniform Rules for Demand Guarantees (URDG), it shall be determined that the content of the said rules constitutes a component of the disputed guarantee. Pursuant to Article 44 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Application of Laws to Foreign-Related Civil Relations, which provides that "tort liability shall be governed by the law of the place of the tort," the standard for determining guarantee fraud, which is not covered by the URDG, shall be governed by the law of the People's Republic of China. China has not acceded to the United Nations Convention on Independent Guarantees and Stand-by Letters of Credit, and the parties in this case have not agreed to apply the said Convention or to incorporate its relevant content as international trading rules into the guarantee. Based on the principle of party autonomy, the United Nations Convention on Independent Guarantees and Stand-by Letters of Credit shall not be applied.

The issue in dispute in this case is whether Waijing Group Company can invoke the "fraud exception" principle to stop payment of the disputed guarantee and the related counter-guarantee. Based on the facts of this case and summarizing the retrial requests and defense opinions of all parties, and as confirmed by the parties during the hearing, this Court's discussion regarding the issues in dispute is as follows:

First, regarding the issue of whether Dongfang Real Estate Company, as beneficiary, has preliminary evidence under the underlying contract to prove that its claim has a factual basis.

This issue concerns the examination of relevant facts under the underlying contract. Both parties in this case claim that the other party was in breach during the performance of the underlying contract, and both assert rights based on the underlying transaction. Therefore, it is necessary to determine whether the beneficiary has preliminary evidence under the underlying contract to prove that its claim has a factual basis. When trying cases involving independent guarantees and related counter-guarantees, the people's court shall adhere to the principles of limitation and necessity in its examination of the underlying transaction. The scope of examination shall be limited to whether the beneficiary knew that the counterparty to the underlying contract did not have any fact of breach under the underlying contract or that there were no other facts giving rise to payment under the independent guarantee. Otherwise, the examination of the underlying contract would undermine the institutional value of the independent guarantee's "pay on first demand" feature.

According to Article 68 of the Opinions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (for Trial Implementation), fraud is mainly manifested as fabricating facts or concealing the truth. Based on the facts found by this Court during retrial, Costa Rica Bank issued performance guarantee No. G051225, which clearly stipulates that the documents required for realization of the guarantee are: supporting documents explaining the reasons for enforcing the guarantee, the date of notification to Waijing Central America Company of the request for enforcement, the original guarantee certificate and any amendments that have been issued. Waijing Group Company claims that Dongfang Real Estate Company's conduct constitutes fraud under the independent guarantee. It must submit evidence to prove that Dongfang Real Estate Company, when realizing the independent guarantee, engaged in one of the following acts: (1) submitting documents that are false in content or forged; (2) submitting a claim that is completely without factual basis and credible support. In this case, the guarantee covered "the quality and durability of materials used during construction, compensation or remedy for losses caused, and/or payment for the contractor's failure to perform obligations." That is, the guarantee covered construction quality and other breaches. Therefore, the beneficiary only needs to submit preliminary evidence capable of proving that there were construction quality issues to satisfy the requirement for realization of the guarantee of "supporting documents explaining the reasons for enforcing the guarantee." During the performance of the underlying contract in this case, Dongfang Real Estate Company's project supervisory personnel, Jose Brenes and Mauricio Mora, issued a "Project Inspection Report" on January 23, 2012. The report found that the construction project had instances of "poor workmanship" and "inferior quality" that required modification or repair. The "Project Inspection Report" constitutes preliminary evidence proving the existence of construction quality issues.

During the retrial of this case, the Foreign Economic Group Company submitted evidence to this Court asserting that Jose Brenes and Mauricio Mora are not international members of the American Institute of Architects, and the Project Engineering Inspection Report signed by them is false. This Court holds that the parties in the Construction Contract and under the guarantee did not expressly stipulate that the Project Engineering Inspection Report must be submitted to the Bank of Costa Rica when realizing the guarantee. Therefore, Orient Real Estate Company has the right to independently choose the type of documentation to submit to the Bank of Costa Rica to "prove the reason for executing the guarantee," and whether it submits the report to the Bank of Costa Rica does not affect the realization of its rights under the guarantee. Moreover, the Construction Contract and the guarantee also did not stipulate that the above report must be issued by AIA International Architects or a person with international membership of the American Institute of Architects. Therefore, whether Jose Brenes and Mauricio Mora have international membership of the American Institute of Architects does not affect their capacity, as the employer's project supervision personnel, to issue the Project Engineering Inspection Report. The judgment of the second instance, on one hand, determined that "Orient Real Estate Company provided the Project Engineering Inspection Report signed by an architect of AIA International Architects," and on the other hand, determined that "the Project Engineering Inspection Report issued by AIA International Architects conflicts with the facts found in the arbitration award made by the arbitral tribunal," thereby confusing the issuing entity of the Project Engineering Inspection Report. This Court hereby corrects this.

This Court notes that among the three new pieces of evidence submitted by the Foreign Economic Group Company to this Court, there are "Progress Payment Detail Tables" for the first to the eighteenth phases of the project involved. In these eighteen "Progress Payment Detail Tables," all are signed by the supervising engineer appointed by Orient Real Estate Company. Among them, the first to ninth phases were solely signed and approved by Mauricio Mora, the tenth phase was solely signed and approved by Jose Brenes, the eleventh, twelfth, and fifteenth phases were jointly signed and approved by Jose Brenes and Kelvin Collado, and the remainder were solely signed and approved by Kelvin Collado. The above evidence was submitted by the Foreign Economic Group Company. During the court hearing of this case, the Foreign Economic Group Company acknowledged the probative effect of the "Progress Payment Detail Tables" and asserted its rights based on them. This Court holds that the Foreign Economic Group Company was aware that both Jose Brenes and Mauricio Mora were project supervision personnel of the employer. When they issued the engineering inspection reports and received the project payments, the Foreign Economic Group Company recognized the supervisory capacity of Jose Brenes and Mauricio Mora. It is logically inconsistent for the Foreign Economic Group Company to use evidence that itself acknowledges and sufficiently proves the supervisory capacity of Jose Brenes and Mauricio Mora to counter-argue that the Project Engineering Inspection Reports issued by Jose Brenes and Mauricio Mora are false. This Court does not support this argument. As the Foreign Economic Group Company failed to provide other evidence proving that Orient Real Estate Company's realization of the guarantee involved in the case was entirely without factual basis or that it submitted false or forged documents, Orient Real Estate Company's application to the Bank of Costa Rica to realize the guarantee rights based on this has a factual basis.

During the retrial, Orient Real Estate Company submitted the first instance judgment No. 150-2016 of the Fourth Civil Court of San Jose, Republic of Costa Rica, intending to prove that this civil judgment had determined that Foreign Economic Central America Company was in material breach of the Construction Contract. Because this judgment was made by a foreign court and has not yet been recognized through China's judicial procedures, it does not have res judicata in proceedings conducted within the territory of China. Moreover, the above judgment has not yet become legally effective and cannot be used as auxiliary evidence in litigation regarding the performance of the underlying transaction.

In summary, the Project Engineering Inspection Report constitutes prima facie evidence proving the Foreign Economic Group Company's breach of contract under the underlying contract. The evidence provided by the Foreign Economic Group Company is insufficient to prove that the above report is false or forged, nor is it sufficient to prove that Orient Real Estate Company knew that the counterparty to the underlying contract did not have any actual breach of contract under the underlying contract or that there was no other fact leading to payment under the independent guarantee, yet still demanded realization of the guarantee. Based on the Foreign Economic Group Company's breach of contract under the underlying contract, and in accordance with the contract's provisions, Orient Real Estate Company's realization of the rights under the independent guarantee does not constitute guarantee fraud. The judgment of the original instance erred in determining that Orient Real Estate Company's claim under the performance guarantee G051225 constituted guarantee fraud. This Court hereby corrects this.

Second, the arbitration award determined that Orient Real Estate Company was in breach of the underlying transaction. As the beneficiary, can Orient Real Estate Company, having been in breach of the underlying contract, still demand realization of the guarantee rights, and should this be considered fraud?

During the hearing of this case, the Foreign Economic Group Company argued that, according to items 3, 4, and 5 of Article 12 of the Supreme People's Court's Provisions on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Independent Guarantee Dispute Cases (hereinafter referred to as the Independent Guarantee Judicial Interpretation), it should be determined that Orient Real Estate Company committed fraud under the independent guarantee. According to Article 25 of the Independent Guarantee Judicial Interpretation, this Court clarified during the hearing that this case is a retrial case under the trial supervision procedure and the provisions of the above judicial interpretation should not apply. After this clarification, the Foreign Economic Group Company still insisted that the spirit of the Independent Guarantee Judicial Interpretation should not be violated. Therefore, based on the facts of this case, this Court provides the following explanation on the relevant issues concerning the Independent Guarantee Judicial Interpretation.

An independent guarantee is independent of the underlying transaction between the principal and the beneficiary. The bank that issues the independent guarantee is only responsible for examining whether the documents submitted by the beneficiary comply with the terms of the guarantee and has the right to decide independently whether to pay. The issuing bank's payment obligation is not affected by the right of defense under the underlying transaction between the principal and the beneficiary. As the beneficiary, when Orient Real Estate Company submits prima facie evidence proving quality issues with the project, even if it has not initiated any dispute resolution procedures such as litigation or arbitration and the counterparty's breach has not been confirmed through such procedures, this does not affect the realization of its guarantee rights. Even if there are ongoing litigation or arbitration proceedings regarding the underlying contract, as long as the relevant dispute resolution procedures have not made a final determination that the debtor of the underlying transaction has no payment or liability obligation, this does not affect the realization of the beneficiary's guarantee rights. Furthermore, even if an effective judgment or arbitration award determines that the beneficiary is in breach of the underlying contract, the existence of such a breach does not necessarily become a sufficient and necessary condition for constituting "fraud" under the guarantee.

In this case, the matters guaranteed by the guarantee are construction quality and other breaches of contract. There is no logical causal relationship between the beneficiary's failure to pay project funds and the occurrence of quality issues. As the beneficiary, Orient Real Estate Company's own breach in the performance of the underlying contract does not necessarily constitute a fraudulent claim under the independent guarantee. The content of item 3, Article 12 of the Independent Guarantee Judicial Interpretation limits the determination of fraud under an independent guarantee to situations where "a court judgment or arbitration award finds that the debtor of the underlying transaction has no payment or liability obligation." Therefore, unless otherwise agreed in the guarantee, the review of the underlying contract should be limited to the performance matters within the scope of the guarantee. When considering whether the beneficiary's own breach in the underlying contract should be included in the review of guarantee fraud, great caution must be exercised. Although the Arbitration Center of the Costa Rican Association of Architects and Engineers issued an arbitration award finding that Orient Real Estate Company breached the contract during performance, the above arbitration proceedings were initiated by the Foreign Economic Group Company on February 7, 2012, and Orient Real Estate Company did not file a counterclaim. The arbitration award made on July 9, 2013, only determined that Orient Real Estate Company was in breach based on the claims of the Foreign Economic Group Company, but did not find that the Foreign Economic Group Company was exempted from payment or liability due to the other party's breach. Therefore, it cannot be determined based on the content of the above arbitration award that Orient Real Estate Company constituted guarantee fraud under item 3, Article 12 of the Independent Guarantee Judicial Interpretation.

In addition, the fact that the parties disputed the project quality and the relevant statements in the Arbitration Award of the Dispute Resolution Center of the Costa Rican Association of Architects and Engineers concerning the project quality issue support the conclusion that the obligations of Foreign Economic Central America Company under the Construction Contract had not been fully performed. There is no situation in this case where Orient Real Estate Company confirmed that the debt under the underlying transaction had been fully performed or that the payment due event had not occurred. The existing evidence also cannot prove that Orient Real Estate Company knowingly abused its rights despite having no right to payment. As the beneficiary, Orient Real Estate Company's own breach in the performance of the underlying contract, although confirmed by the arbitration award, did not thereby exempt the Foreign Economic Group Company from payment or liability. In summary, even applying the Independent Guarantee Judicial Interpretation as argued by the Foreign Economic Group Company, the circumstances of this case do not constitute guarantee fraud. The judgment of the second instance held that the Arbitration Award of the Dispute Resolution Center of the Costa Rican Association of Architects and Engineers did not find that Foreign Economic Central America Company had serious breach issues in construction, and that the Project Engineering Inspection Report conflicted with the facts found by the arbitration award. Based on this, the second instance judgment determined that Orient Real Estate Company committed fraud in the performance of the guarantee, which lacks factual basis. This Court hereby corrects this.

Third, concerning the issue of the independent counter-guarantee related to the independent guarantee in this case.

In this case, after the Foreign Economic Group Company applied to China Construction Bank, Anhui Branch, and used the Bank of Costa Rica as the issuing bank to issue the performance guarantee G051225 to the beneficiary, Orient Real Estate Company, China Construction Bank, Anhui Branch, as the guarantor, issued the counter-guarantee No. 34147020000289 to the Bank of Costa Rica, promising to pay the amount under the guarantee within twenty days of receiving notice from the Bank of Costa Rica. After Orient Real Estate Company submitted a claim statement to the Bank of Costa Rica, the Bank of Costa Rica informed China Construction Bank, Anhui Branch of Orient Real Estate Company's claim. After the Second Chamber of the Administrative Litigation Court of Costa Rica issued an order for temporary protection measures, the Bank of Costa Rica suspended the execution of performance guarantee G051225. On March 6, 2012, the Second Chamber of the Administrative Litigation Court of Costa Rica lifted the order for temporary protection measures. On March 20, 2012, at the request of the Bank of Costa Rica, China Construction Bank, Anhui Branch extended the validity period of independent counter-guarantee No. 34147020000289. On March 21, 2012, the Bank of Costa Rica paid the amount under guarantee G051225 to Orient Real Estate Company.

Based on the characteristics of an independent guarantee, the guarantor constitutes a direct payment obligation to the beneficiary separate from the debtor. The independent guarantee has no dependency on the principal obligation regarding the right of defense. Even if the debtor exercises the right of defense in a certain dispute resolution procedure, it does not necessarily entitle the independent guarantor to obtain that defense benefit. Furthermore, even if there is a situation of fraudulent claim by the beneficiary under the independent guarantee, it cannot be presumed that the issuing bank constitutes a fraudulent claim under the independent counter-guarantee. Only when the issuing bank knowingly pays despite the beneficiary's fraudulent claim and in violation of the principle of good faith, and then claims payment from the counter-guarantor under the independent counter-guarantee, can the issuing bank be determined to have made a fraudulent claim under the independent counter-guarantee.

The Foreign Economic Group Company initiated this lawsuit on the grounds of guarantee fraud. It must prove that the Bank of Costa Rica knowingly paid despite Orient Real Estate Company's fraud under the independent guarantee, in violation of the principle of good faith, and then, as the beneficiary, made a claim under the sight-demand independent counter-guarantee, constituting a fraudulent claim under the counter-guarantee. The Foreign Economic Group Company not only failed to prove that the Bank of Costa Rica's payment to Orient Real Estate Company under the independent guarantee was fraudulent, but also failed to provide evidence proving that the Bank of Costa Rica made a fraudulent claim under the independent counter-guarantee. Its claim to stop payment of the amount under the independent counter-guarantee has no factual basis.

In summary, the Foreign Economic Group Company cannot prove that Orient Real Estate Company committed fraud under the independent guarantee, nor that the Bank of Costa Rica knowingly paid despite Orient Real Estate Company's fraud under the independent guarantee, in violation of the principle of good faith. The Foreign Economic Group Company's claim to stop payment of the amounts under the independent guarantee and the independent counter-guarantee in this case has no factual basis. The judgments of the first and second instances erred in finding facts and applying law, and should be corrected. Pursuant to Article 170, Paragraph 1, Item 2, and Article 207, Paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 407, Paragraph 2 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, this Court hereby renders the following judgment:

1. The Civil Judgment (2014) Wan Min Er Zhong Zi No. 00389 of the Anhui High People's Court and the Civil Judgment (2012) He Min Si Chu Zi No. 00005 of the Hefei Intermediate People's Court are hereby vacated;

2. The claims of Anhui Foreign Economic Construction (Group) Co., Ltd. are hereby dismissed.

The first instance case acceptance fee of RMB 97,693, the property preservation fee of RMB 5,000, and the second instance case acceptance fee of RMB 97,493, are all to be borne by Anhui Foreign Economic Construction (Group) Co., Ltd.

This judgment is final.
